comparison: Perfect agreement on C1-C3. Both evaluations find the evidence for cDC1 accumulation in atherosclerotic lesions (human and mouse) fully supported. OpenEval emphasizes the complementary techniques and statistical significance, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the findings as 'convincingly revealed.'

Strong agreement on C4-C7, C88. Both evaluations support the novel mouse model for selective cDC1 targeting. OpenEval provides detailed validation assessment, while peer reviewers explicitly praise the methodological advance and note it avoids 'off-target activity.' Both treat this as a key contribution.

Both address C76 regarding the mouse model clarifying cDC1's role. Peer R13 focuses specifically on this methodological contribution claim, while OpenEval R2 includes it as part of broader model validation. Complete agreement on the significance of the new genetic model.

Agreement on C8, C12 regarding reduced atherosclerosis. Both find the lesion reduction well-supported. OpenEval R3 also covers C9-C11 (negative findings on confounders), which peer reviewers address separately in R4, showing slightly different grouping strategies but consistent evaluation.

Both address C9-C11 regarding unchanged macrophage content and lipid metabolism. Complete agreement that these negative findings support the specificity of cDC1's role. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'cDC1 depletion did not alter macrophage populations.'

Strong agreement on C13-C16, C20 regarding tissue-specific T cell activation effects. Both find the aortic T cell activation reduction well-supported. OpenEval notes the causal link remains correlative, while peer reviewers accept the findings without raising this concern.

Agreement on C17-C19, C79-C80 regarding systemic and diet-dependent T cell effects. Both evaluations support these findings. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through overall positive assessment, while OpenEval explicitly notes these add complexity to the interpretation.

Both address C81-C82 regarding mechanistic interpretations of cDC1-T cell interactions. OpenEval rates these as correlative rather than mechanistically proven, while peer reviewers implicitly support the interpretative framework, noting results 'imply cellular interactions.' Subtle difference in confidence level.

Perfect agreement on C21-C23, C26. Both evaluations fully support the bone marrow origin findings and specificity validation. OpenEval emphasizes this resolves a key question, while peer reviewers implicitly validate through acceptance of the overall model.

Strong agreement on C24-C25, C27, C68-C69, C73-C75 regarding tissue-specific cDC1 heterogeneity from scRNA-seq. Both find the data well-supported. OpenEval notes the limitation of small cell numbers (68 cells), while peer reviewers raise no concerns about the single-cell data.

Agreement on C70-C72 regarding HFD-induced changes in splenic cDC1. Both evaluations support these findings. Peer R8 groups these with aortic heterogeneity data, while OpenEval R7 treats them separately, focusing on the mechanistic insights about hyperlipidemia effects.

Both address C96-C97 regarding causal inferences from scRNA-seq data. OpenEval finds the inference reasonable given experimental design, while peer reviewers implicitly support through positive overall assessment. Agreement on the validity of these interpretative claims.

Strong agreement on C28-C30, C83-C87 regarding Xcl1-Xcr1 axis targeting. Both evaluations strongly support these findings. Peer reviewers call the XCL1 results 'surprising' and 'very important,' while OpenEval notes the striking efficacy despite only partial cDC1 reduction.

Agreement on C31-C32 regarding selective effects of Xcl1 deletion. Both support these findings showing more limited effects than complete cDC1 depletion. OpenEval emphasizes the contrast suggesting compensatory mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept within the 'non-redundant role' framework.

Agreement on C33-C35 regarding differential effects of Xcl1 deletion versus complete cDC1 depletion. Both evaluations support the distinction. OpenEval emphasizes compensatory mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept this as consistent with the non-redundant role of the XCL1-XCR1 axis.

Agreement on C77-C78 regarding preserved lymphoid organ populations with Xcl1 deletion. Both evaluations support these negative findings as demonstrating specificity. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through overall positive assessment of Xcl1 work.

Divergence on C36, C60-C61. OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting mechanistic explanations are speculative and the discrepancy between depletion approaches is observed but not resolved. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting the mechanistic framework without raising concerns.

Divergence on C62-C64 regarding mechanistic speculation and therapeutic potential. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting therapeutic target identification is premature and mechanisms are speculative. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, endorsing therapeutic implications through positive overall assessment of XCL1 findings.

Both address C59, C67 regarding Xcl1 as therapeutic target. OpenEval includes these in UNCERTAIN evaluation, noting premature therapeutic claims. Peer R9 groups with broader Xcl1 findings rated as SUPPORTED, emphasizing 'very important gain in knowledge.' Clear divergence in confidence about therapeutic implications.

Peer R3 addresses C65-C66 (claims about lesion numbers and size reduction) which are not explicitly covered in any OpenEval result. These appear to be specific quantitative details that OpenEval grouped within broader atherosclerosis reduction findings.
